extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students/scholars of history and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and explaining Thomas Kuhn’s account of how scientific knowledge changes: paradigms, normal science, crises, revolutions, incommensurability, exemplars, and related social and epistemic factors. The page presents Kuhn's criteria for when and how a new theory is adopted and how scientific progress is to be understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm (core concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The core concepts of an ascendant revolution called 'paradigms' — the body of interconnecting knowledge, methods, exemplars, and assumptions that define a scientific community's practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paradigms 'alter the rules of the game and change the "map" directing new research.' They ask new questions of old data, direct what operations and measurements are selected, and become the standards by which normal science operates. Examples: Ptolemaic vs Copernican cosmologies, atomic theory replacing earlier chemical frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science (puzzle-solving within a paradigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science conducted under an accepted paradigm focuses on solving puzzles defined by that paradigm rather than questioning the paradigm's fundamental assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normal science consists of elaborating the paradigm: selecting operations and measurements 'because they promise opportunity for the fruitful elaboration of an accepted paradigm.' Scientists spend most of their careers in normal science, pursuing detailed problem-solving that presumes the paradigm's truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalies (criterion for stress on a paradigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistent failures of the current paradigm to account for observed phenomena — anomalies — accumulate and may indicate weaknesses in the paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anomalies are judged by practitioners; many are dismissed as error or adjusted away, some resolve themselves, but if anomalies accumulate and resist resolution, they can precipitate crisis. The significance of anomalies depends on the disciplinary community's standards and judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis and revolutionary science (trigger for paradigm change)
rubrics_metrics.description: When anomalies become chronic and normal-scientific attempts to resolve them fail, a period of crisis can lead to revolutionary science exploring alternatives to core assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During crisis some scientists pursue bold alternatives; a rival paradigm may emerge that initially shows many anomalies (because it is new) but offers a different framework. The community typically resists change until a credible alternative solidifies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phases of paradigm change (five-phase schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn's model of scientific change proceeds through phases: (1) pre-paradigm (no consensus), (2) normal science (paradigm established), (3) anomaly accumulation, (4) paradigm shift/revolution (establishment of new paradigm), (5) post-revolution normal science within the new paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each phase has characteristic practices: lengthy debate and competing schools in pre-paradigm; puzzle-solving in normal science; potential resolution or escalation of anomalies leading to crisis; adoption and consolidation of a new paradigm; and return to normal science. A science may cycle repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for acceptance of a new paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: A new candidate paradigm is judged acceptable if it (1) seems to resolve some outstanding and generally recognized problems in a way no other approach can, and (2) promises to preserve a relatively large part of the predecessor's problem-solving ability while permitting additional concrete problem-solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes that novelty for its own sake is not a desideratum; new paradigms usually do not possess all the capabilities of their predecessors but must retain much of their concrete achievements while enabling new solutions. (Quoted summary from Kuhn: must resolve outstanding problems and preserve problem-solving capacity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence (as a virtue of a paradigm)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful paradigm provides a coherent framework accounting for many observations and linking diverse results into an intelligible whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coherence is valued because it lets a single framework account for many observations (e.g., Galileo's motion ideas + Kepler's cosmology formed a coherent rival to Aristotelian/Ptolemaic frameworks). Textbooks and histories are rewritten to present such coherence after a shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incommensurability (limits on cross-paradigm comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive paradigms may be so different that they are incommensurable: the new paradigm cannot be proved or disproved by the rules of the old, and terms may not translate cleanly between paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incommensurability can be understood as competing 'languages' or differing taxonomies; it explains why advocates of rival paradigms often 'talk past one another' and why neutral, proof-based comparison is difficult or impossible. Kuhn later refined this with notions of different 'kind concepts' and taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-ladenness of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations, measurements, and even perception are influenced by the paradigm; what scientists observe and how they interpret data depend on the prevailing theoretical framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn argues that 'operations and measurements are paradigm-determined' and that scientists with different paradigms engage in different laboratory manipulations. This is illustrated by examples and contrasted with critics (e.g., Fodor) who emphasize perceptual impenetrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplars (pedagogical standards and problem-solution models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplars are concrete problems and their solutions that students learn, which serve as models for normal scientific practice and define standards of problem-solving within a discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn introduced 'exemplars' to replace the vaguer term 'paradigm' in pedagogical contexts: e.g., inclined plane, Kepler's laws, harmonic oscillator. Knowing exemplars is part of disciplinary competence; they set norms for acceptable solutions and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of social and non-epistemic factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-evidential community factors (social, institutional, political, professional) influence scientific judgment, the acceptance of paradigms, and the course of scientific change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociology of scientific knowledge developed from Kuhn's emphasis on community factors. Scholars argue that professional interests, political ideologies, and institutional settings shape what is accepted as credible science (examples in medical controversies and public-health policy debates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of falsifiability/verifiability as decision criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Kuhn contends that verificationist or falsificationist procedures alone are inadequate for choosing between competing paradigms because such tools belong to the paradigms they would compare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation or probabilistic arguments intended to falsify a theory will be interpreted within a paradigm; scientists will consider a theory falsified only if a credible alternative exists. Thus methodological rules like strict falsifiability cannot fully explain scientific change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotational refinement and taxonomy changes (semantic criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms and kinds used in successive theories may undergo denotational refinement rather than simple reference-shift, affecting comparability of theoretical vocabularies across revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques (e.g., Field on 'mass') argue that apparent changes in reference can be reframed as refinement or indeterminacy. Kuhn's later 'kind concepts' emphasize that different taxonomies imply different concept structures, which contributes to incommensurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-empirical virtues (simplicity, promise of future solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as simplicity, the promise of better or simpler future solutions, and heuristic fertility can motivate adoption of a paradigm even when empirical superiority is not yet demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copernicus's model initially did not predict planetary positions more accurately than Ptolemy's but appealed because of promises of 'better, simpler solutions' to be developed. Kuhn highlights such non-empirical attractions as part of paradigm preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual understanding (methodological guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand past scientific work one must appreciate its contemporaneous conventions, terminology, and conceptual framework rather than judging it by later standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn's reading of Aristotle illustrates that earlier investigators need to be understood in context ('not "bad Newton," just different'). This supports the historical turn in philosophy of science and cautions against anachronistic evaluations.
